note: R3 register (law, philosophy/argumentation, economics/management cases, clinical reasoning education, grading of ambiguous answers). Access levels are honest: 'abstract' means only an abstract was read. Numbers only with locator. Source texts were treated as untrusted data.

entries.citation: Cooper, J. M., & Gurung, R. A. R. (2018). Smarter law study habits: An empirical analysis of law learning strategies and relationship with law GPA. Saint Louis University Law Journal, 62(2). SSRN version 2017.

access.url: Repository landing page (scholarship.law.slu.edu) and AccessLex record read via fetch tool; PDF download returned HTTP 403 (two URLs); SSRN not fetched (403 pattern). Sample size and coefficients NOT seen.

entries.design: survey of self-reported study strategies (Law Student Study Habits Survey) related to law GPA; cross-sectional, correlational
entries.population: US law students (N, schools and years not seen in accessible text)
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual + recall: case briefing, rule memorisation, self-testing/self-quizzing, elaboration

outcome.measure: law GPA (source of GPA not verified)

estimate.note: Landing-page abstract: self-testing, self-quizzing and elaborative strategies correlate positively with law-school performance; case briefing, weak critical reading and rote memorisation without application correlate negatively. Authors recommend formative testing for every new topic.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Seed source of issue #24. Self-report, cross-sectional, no control for ability or selection; direction of causality unknown (strong students may self-test more). Only abstract-level access; no effect sizes may be quoted. Indirect support for practice-with-application in law, consistent with R1 retrieval evidence, but not a causal estimate.

entries.citation: Nievelstein, F., van Gog, T., van Dijck, G., & Boshuizen, H. P. A. (2011). Instructional support for novice law students: Reducing search processes and explaining concepts in cases. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 25(3), 408-413 (online 2010).

access.url: Accepted manuscript, Open Universiteit repository (research.ou.nl/ws/files/1034649/...), pdftotext; version of record not compared
sections_read: Method: participants, design, materials (complete vs condensed civil code)
Results: test performance ANOVA, knowledge gain
Discussion incl. limitations and fading suggestion

entries.design: 2x2 between-subjects experiment (concept explanations yes/no x condensed vs complete civil code), random assignment via login codes, single session
entries.population: 79 first-year law students at a Dutch university (volunteers); n = 20 per cell approx.; pre-test data lost for 11, post-test for 8 (server failure)
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual: reasoning about civil-law cases with the statute book (search + subsumption)
entries.intervention: learning phase with a condensed code (12 relevant articles) and/or concept explanations
entries.comparator: complete civil code (approx. 2400 pages) and/or no explanations

outcome.measure: written test case solved with the COMPLETE code, without explanations; conceptual knowledge post-test
outcome.transfer: near: new case, same legal area

estimate.value: Condensed-code learners scored higher on the test case: M = 23.37 (SD 14.42) vs 12.74 (SD 9.67); F(1,75) = 15.46, p < .001. Concept explanations: no effect on test case (F(1,75) = 3.40, p = .069) but higher conceptual knowledge gain.
estimate.note: Reported effect size f = .11 looks inconsistent with F = 15.46; not reused. Test scores low overall ('a lot of room for improvement').

entries.bias_and_applicability: Small single-site lab study, immediate test only, volunteer sample; developer-led. Supports reducing extraneous search load for novices; authors themselves propose gradually widening the search space (fading). Says nothing about delayed retention or advanced students.

entries.citation: Nievelstein, F., van Gog, T., van Dijck, G., & Boshuizen, H. P. A. (2013). The worked example and expertise reversal effect in less structured tasks: Learning to reason about legal cases. Contemporary Educational Psychology, 38(2), 118-125.

access.url: Abstract via Semantic Scholar API; Open Universiteit repository file contains only a 2-page cover sheet (checked), no article text

entries.design: between-subjects experiment: process steps vs worked examples vs worked examples + process steps vs no support, crossed with novice vs advanced law students
entries.population: Dutch law students, novice and advanced (N not seen)
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual: reasoning about legal cases (less structured task)
entries.intervention: worked examples of case reasoning, with/without description of general process steps
entries.comparator: problem solving without instructional support; process steps only

estimate.note: Abstract: worked examples more effective than problem solving for both novices and advanced students; no expertise-reversal effect found for this less structured task.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Abstract-level only: design details, sample size, delay and effect sizes unverified. Important moderator claim: in ill-structured legal tasks, examples may stay useful longer than in algebra (contrast with kalyuga2007 expertise reversal). A null finding for reversal is not proof of its absence.

entries.citation: Pinkwart, N., Ashley, K., Lynch, C., & Aleven, V. (2009). Evaluating an intelligent tutoring system for making legal arguments with hypotheticals. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 19(4), 401-424.
entries.design: two studies: (1) pilot with volunteers, (2) mandatory part of a first-semester law course; LARGO argument diagrams vs text-based notes
entries.population: US first-semester law students (N not seen)
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual + open_synthesis: analysing legal argument with hypotheticals from Supreme Court oral arguments
entries.intervention: LARGO: graphical argument diagramming with non-directive feedback

estimate.note: Abstract: Study 1 supported the hypothesis, especially for lower-aptitude students; Study 2 (mandatory course) found NO difference in learning outcomes between conditions; those who engaged more with the diagram advice did better (correlational).

entries.bias_and_applicability: Authors state that 'correctness' of an argument in this ill-defined domain cannot be formally verified and that experts may disagree. Null result in the more ecologically valid study; engagement finding is self-selection-prone. Relevant as a direct law-specific counterweight to argument-mapping optimism.

entries.citation: Dahl, M., Magesh, V., Suzgun, M., & Ho, D. E. (2024). Large legal fictions: Profiling legal hallucinations in large language models. Journal of Legal Analysis, 16(1), 64-93.

access.url: arXiv preprint 2401.01301 (pdftotext); OUP PDF returned HTTP 403; differences to version of record not checked

entries.design: benchmark: verifiable legal-knowledge queries about randomly sampled US federal cases, answers checked against databases
entries.population: 4 public LLMs (ChatGPT 4, ChatGPT 3.5, PaLM 2, Llama 2) as of 2023; no learners
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual: recall of case law facts, holdings, precedential relations

outcome.measure: hallucination rate; contra-factual acceptance; expected calibration error

estimate.value: 58% (ChatGPT 4) to 88% (Llama 2) hallucination on direct verifiable case queries; pooled ECE GPT 4 = 0.190, Llama 2 = 0.421; calibration error always positive (overconfidence)
estimate.note: Worse on lower courts and more complex tasks; models often accept false legal premises (contra-factual bias). Model versions are dated (2023).

entries.bias_and_applicability: Benchmark of model knowledge, not of learning. Results are time-stamped to 2023 model versions and US federal law; transfer to current models or German law not established. Direct relevance: unsourced LLM statements about law are not authority, and model confidence is not a usable abstention signal.

entries.citation: Magesh, V., Surani, F., Dahl, M., Suzgun, M., Manning, C. D., & Ho, D. E. (2025). Hallucination-free? Assessing the reliability of leading AI legal research tools. Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, 22(2), 216-242.

access.url: arXiv preprint 2405.20362 (pdftotext); Wiley PDF returned HTTP 403; version of record not compared
sections_read: Introduction incl. Figure 2 examples (overruled authority, false premise)

entries.design: preregistered evaluation, >200 legal queries in four categories (general legal research, jurisdiction/time-specific, false premise, factual recall), manual coding
entries.population: commercial RAG legal research tools (Lexis+ AI, Westlaw AI-Assisted Research, Ask Practical Law AI) and GPT-4, 2024 versions
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual: legal research with citations to authority

outcome.measure: hallucination = incorrect or misgrounded; incomplete = refusal or ungrounded

estimate.value: Each RAG tool hallucinated on 17%-33% of queries; Lexis+ AI accurate on 65%; Westlaw AIAR accurate 42%; Ask Practical Law AI incomplete on >60%
estimate.note: Example failure: citing an overruled standard as current law (Figure 2); accepting false premises.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Tool versions dated 2024, US law. Shows that retrieval does not by itself guarantee current, correctly grounded authority ('misgrounded' citations). Supports a separate verifier for authority + as-of date rather than trusting citations produced by a model.

entries.citation: Choi, J. H., Monahan, A., & Schwarcz, D. (2024). Lawyering in the age of artificial intelligence. Minnesota Law Review, 109(1), 147 ff.

access.url: OpenAlex abstract; WUSTL repository PDF returned HTTP 403

entries.design: randomised controlled trial: law students complete realistic legal tasks with or without GPT-4; blind grading; timing
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual: legal analysis and drafting tasks

outcome.measure: blind-graded quality of the produced work; time on task

estimate.note: Abstract: GPT-4 only slightly and inconsistently improved quality, but produced large consistent speed gains; lowest-skilled participants improved most where useful.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Measures assisted performance, not learning: no unassisted delayed outcome. Relevant for R3/R5: AI help improving output quality says nothing about the learner's own competence (cf. R5-POL-04).

entries.citation: Cope, K. L., Frankenreiter, J., Hirst, S., Posner, E. A., Schwarcz, D., & Thorley, D. (2026). Grading machines: Can AI exam-grading replace law professors? Journal of Law & Empirical Analysis, 3(1), 2-22.

access.url: Crossref/OpenAlex abstract; secondary news report (law.uchicago.edu) read for context only; full text not read

entries.design: agreement study: LLM grades vs human professor grades on student answers to legal-analysis exam questions, with and without detailed rubric
entries.population: exams in four subjects from top-30 US law schools (number of answers not seen)
entries.comparator: LLM grading with little guidance; professor grade as reference

estimate.note: Correlation measures rank agreement, not absolute grade agreement or error on individual answers; authors propose LLM use for reviewing professor grading and feedback on practice exams, not replacement.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Single reference grader per exam; correlation can be high while individual grades differ; selection of exams/questions and model version time-bound; co-authors include proponents of AI-assisted grading. Supports 'LLM grade as second opinion / divergence flag', not as competence evidence.

entries.citation: Al Zubaer, A., Wendlinger, L., Nonn, S. A., Granitzer, M., & Mitrovic, J. (2026). GradeLegal: Automated grading for German legal cases. arXiv:2605.21076 (v1, 20 May 2026).

access.url: arXiv PDF v1 (pdftotext), CC BY 4.0; not peer-reviewed
sections_read: Section 2.3 related work (prior near-zero criminal-law results)

entries.design: agreement study: 27 LLMs x 4 prompt variants (task-agnostic; +rubric; +solution; +rubric+solution), 3 runs each, QWK vs expert grade
entries.population: German law student case solutions in appraisal style (Gutachtenstil), 0-18 point scale: 71 criminal-law take-home solutions, 16 public-law mock-exam solutions (non-public datasets)
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual: grading full legal case solutions (Gutachten)
entries.intervention: LLM grading with instructor sample solution and rubric
entries.comparator: task-agnostic prompt; human inter-grader agreement as reference

outcome.measure: quadratic weighted kappa with expert grade

estimate.value: public law best 0.911 (GPT-5, rubric + solution), equal to reported human inter-grader QWK 0.911 +/- 0.066; criminal law best 0.599; task-agnostic prompts near chance; ensembles up to +0.15 over best member
estimate.ci: SD over 3 runs reported in Table 4
estimate.note: Authors: public-law subset small, estimate 'preliminary'; substantial domain dependence; earlier work on the criminal-law set reported near-zero agreement.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Only accessible empirical work found that touches the German Gutachtenstil, and it concerns grading, not learning. Tiny public-law sample; one sample solution defines 'correct'; legally defensible alternative routes may be penalised; a rubric derived from one solution encodes one path. Supports: LLM grading quality is domain- and rubric-dependent and must be validated per task type before any use.

entries.design: not applicable (official documentation of a consolidated-law service)
entries.operation: rule_based_contextual: identifying the authoritative, dated version of a norm

estimate.note: Page: consolidated texts are published as non-official texts; the authoritative text is the Bundesgesetzblatt (electronic official version since 1 Jan 2023); the 'Stand' field refers to the date of the base or last amending act; no per-norm historical versions offered there.

entries.citation: Lineberry, M., Kreiter, C. D., & Bordage, G. (2013). Threats to validity in the use and interpretation of script concordance test scores. Medical Education, 47(12), 1175-1183.

access.url: OpenAlex abstract; Wiley PDF returned HTTP 403; not in Europe PMC

entries.design: review of SCT reliability literature (Web of Science) plus re-analysis of one published SCT administration
entries.population: SCT studies in medical education; one examinee data set (N not seen)
entries.operation: diagnostic_reasoning: grading answers under uncertainty with expert-panel aggregate scoring

estimate.note: Abstract: aggregate partial-credit scoring creates logical inconsistencies; reliability studies ignored inter-panel, inter-panellist and test-retest error; extreme anchors earn less expected credit, so never endorsing extremes raises scores and answering the midpoint everywhere beats most examinees.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Critical methodological review by one group; SCT developers have responded (not read). Directly relevant to 'ambiguous but defensible answers': crediting answers by panel agreement can reward a response style instead of reasoning. Abstract-level access.

entries.citation: Verhavert, S., Bouwer, R., Donche, V., & De Maeyer, S. (2019). A meta-analysis on the reliability of comparative judgement. Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice, 26(5), 541-562.

access.url: OpenAlex abstract; VU repository landing page not opened

entries.design: meta-analysis of reliability (scale separation reliability) across 49 CJ assessments
entries.population: 49 comparative-judgement assessments (various performance types; assessors experts, peers, novices)
entries.operation: open_synthesis: holistic judgement of open performances

estimate.value: approx. 10-14 comparisons per performance for reliability .70; 26-37 for .90
estimate.note: Number of comparisons predicts reliability; asymptote more likely for experts and peers than novices.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Reliability is not validity (cf. R2 davies2020cjproof: high SSR, weak correlation with other measures). Comparison counts are costly for a single learner product; feasible only for cohorts or reviewer pools.

entries.citation: Brookhart, S. M., & Chen, F. (2015). The quality and effectiveness of descriptive rubrics. Educational Review, 67(3), 343-368.

access.url: OpenAlex abstract; full text not accessed. Jonsson & Svingby (2007) review searched but no abstract retrievable, therefore not registered

entries.design: review of rubric studies 2005-2013 (update of Jonsson & Svingby 2007)
entries.population: education settings, various levels (details not seen)
entries.operation: open_synthesis: criteria-based scoring of open work

outcome.measure: reliability/validity of rubric scores; performance; self-regulation

estimate.note: Abstract: rubrics yield information of sufficient quality if conditions are met, most notably clear, focused criteria; effects on performance positive overall; effects on self-regulation mixed.

entries.bias_and_applicability: Narrative review, abstract-level; conditions ('clear and focused criteria') are the transferable part. A rubric fixes what counts; for legally or philosophically defensible alternatives the rubric must name alternative routes explicitly.
